one_sentence_failure_summary: The agent oscillated between a regex-based approach that corrupted HTML attribute syntax and a BeautifulSoup approach whose serialization changed indentation and tag structure, never converging on an implementation that was both complete in JS removal and format-preserving.
t_err_evidence: At step 17 the agent commits to a regex-only implementation to 'preserve formatting', adopting the false premise that regex can reliably match and remove HTML attributes containing nested quotes; the `[^'"]*` pattern cannot handle single quotes inside double-quoted attribute values such as `onclick="alert('Clicked!')"`, making HTML corruption inevitable.
t_commit_evidence: At step 33 the agent rewrites to BeautifulSoup with html.parser but adds line-by-line re-indentation logic and empty-tag cleanup via regex, permanently encoding both formatting-change violations and incomplete JS vector coverage; all subsequent iterations (steps 42, 45) retain BS4 serialization that changes formatting while still missing iframe/object/embed removal.
t_surface_evidence: At step 21 the filtered test.html shows broken tag syntax: `<h1Clicked!')>` and `<pMouse over!')>`, proving the regex event-handler removal consumed part of the attribute value rather than the complete attribute.
trigger_explanation: The agent assumed at step 16-17 that targeted regex substitutions could reliably remove HTML event-handler attributes while preserving all surrounding content. This premise is false: the regex `\s+(onclick|...)\s*=\s*["'][^"']*["']` cannot correctly match attributes whose values contain the opposite quote type (e.g., double-quoted attribute with single-quoted JS string), leading to partial matches that corrupt the surrounding tag.
forewarning_evidence: At step 9, after the first BeautifulSoup+lxml run, the filtered test.html showed significant formatting changes (indentation stripped, attribute order changed, self-closing tags added) compared to the original — a clear signal that any parser-based approach changes formatting, which the agent correctly diagnosed at step 11 but then tried to fix via regex (the wrong direction).
